Ford Patents Idea That Lets Parked Cars Autonomously Flee Danger

MR
By Marco Rossi Senior Supercar & Aerodynamics Editor • via Car and Driver Wire
⚡ Visual Story
Source & Photography: Car and Driver Wire Dispatch Verified Editorial Asset
⚡ Executive Takeaways & Key Highlights
  • It’s usually not a good sign when you park your car and then return to that spot to find it’s not where you left it.
  • An idea in a recently published Ford patent application would turn that into a positive, though, as it would mean the vehicle sensed trouble and autonomously re-parked itself somewhere it deemed safer.
  • Official reporting verified via Car and Driver news desk.
⚡ EDITORIAL TAKE • MARCO ROSSI Senior Supercar & Aerodynamics Editor

The Benchmark for Track-Tolerant Engineering

In the high-stakes supercar arena, pure horsepower is no longer enough to claim supremacy. This dispatch from Car and Driver emphasizes how cutting-edge downforce balance, electronic limited-slip differentials, and hybrid torque-vectoring are reshaping driver engagement. Exotic marques must prove that extreme performance can harmonize with reliability, thermal endurance, and road compliance.

Big Picture: Lap times at benchmark proving grounds and early client allocations will reveal whether this performance envelope disrupts the existing supercar hierarchy.

It’s usually not a good sign when you park your car and then return to that spot to find it’s not where you left it. An idea in a recently published Ford patent application would turn that into a positive, though, as it would mean the vehicle sensed trouble and autonomously re-parked itself somewhere it deemed safer. The patent also describes ways to park and safeguard specific pieces of vehicle equipment—such as the wheels—and what you’re carrying inside or in a pickup’s bed.

📌 The Core Development

A Ford patent application submitted to the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) explains that a vehicle would detect “suspicious activity” and relocate itself somewhere less sketchy. Examples of these potential threats include a person who keeps peering into the windows or another vehicle repeatedly circling. The system could also decide a new spot is in order if the car finds itself alone in a previously populated lot—our four-wheeled friends get lonely too.

🔍 Background & Sector Context

In a less complicated implementation, the vehicle could recommend a parking location and/or orientation to the driver, who would then park manually to, ideally, reduce the likelihood of theft.

📊 Industry & Real-World Impact

Alone with fleeing danger, the application describes a variety of ways the vehicle could park itself for self-preservation. Most of these methods are intended to prevent wheel theft, a very real threat to new vehicles. (One of our test cars fell victim when it was minding its own business in a staffer’s suburban carport one moment, unceremoniously left wheelless on a pair of landscaping blocks the next.)
